speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: On the motion of Hon. W. T. White for Committee of Supply:

speakeroldname: Mr. J. J. CARRICK (Thunder Bay and Rainy River):
speechtext:
Before the House goes into Committee of Supply I would like to draw attention to a subject which I believe to be of vital importance to the industrial development and commercial life of the Dominion of Canada. I refer to our Canadian iron and steel industry.
A few weeks ago I placed a resolution on the Order Paper under which I proposed to draw attention to this subject, but in view of the fact that so many other notices of motion preceded it, I did not think I would Have an opportunity of bringing the matter up for some time, so, with the consent of the Prime Minister, I dropped the resolution and wish to take the matter up now. The notice of motion reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, it would be in the best interests of Canada that the development and utilization of Canadian iron ore deposits should be more fully encouraged 
than they are at present; and that this House will approve and support any legislative measures proposed by the Government that would tend to so desirable an end.
The iron and steel industry is second only to agriculture in the foremost countries of the civilized world. Iron is the cheapest and most abundant of heavy metals; it is the strongest and most magnetic of known substances and perhaps, the most indis-pensible of all materials to human progress, excepting the water we drink and the air we breathe. It enters into every industry; it is the basic fibre of our national existence. It is indispensible to the tiller of the soil, to the hewer of wood, the manufacturer of flour, foods and feed, the miner of coal, the builder of street cars, motorcars, telephones, telegraphs, steamships and railways. All need iron both as instrument and material and all would fail if iron failed. Without iron we could have no important industries; it is the basic fibre of our industrial existence.
Another exemplification of the great need . for assistance to the iron industry is found in the fact that during the fiscal year 1913 there were imported into Canada iron and steel products amounting to the enormous sum of $141,000,000. This importation constitute? nearly one-quarter of the total amount of imports into the Dominion of Canada during the fiscal year 1913. What would it mean to the development and prosperity of Canada if this vast amount of iron and steel, or even a substantial portion of it, were manufactured in our own factories and steel plants, and from our own iron deposits?
Another reason why this matter should engage the attention of the House is that the iron situation in Canada to-day is in a languishing and deplorable condition. Instead of making progress, instead of developing our natural resources, we are steadily retrogressing. During the past year we produced 50 per cent less Canadian iron ore than we did ten years ago, but the imports of foreign ores have increased over 250 per cent. Canadian blast furnaces are closed down, and we are keeping busy United States furnaces and United States steel plants by importing their products. The blast furnace at Port Arthur represents an investment of over $1,000,000. The citizens of that city were so anxious to help that industry and the development of iron in their district that they guaranteed _ the bonds of the company to the extent of $200,000. This huge furnace-a modern plant, constructed by British and Canadian

capital and assisted by the credit of the city of Port Arthur-has been closed down for two years. Nor is this a solitary instance. The blast furnaces at Midland, Parry Sound, Deseronto and Londonderry are closed down. These plants represent an investment of millions of dollars; they gave employment to thousands of our Canadian citizens; they paid out hundreds of thousands of dollars in wages. To-day they are all idle; they are in mourning for the passing of an infant industry which, with sufficient assistance, would have developed into giant proportions. These huge idle furnaces, with their great towering steel structures, are sepulchral monuments marking the sad record of loss and disappointment, of blasted hopes and shattered fortunes.
Our Canadian industries have been unable to withstand the competition of the older and more strongly established industries of the United 5 p.m. States. The United States and other foreign countries have so protected their industries that they have secured their own home markets for them, and have been able to use Canada as a dumping ground for their surplus products.
During the past week the Hamilton Steel Company closed down its large plant, turning 1,300 men out of employment. What a severe blow it is to a young and thriving industrial city when 1,300 men are turned out of a single industry- men who are depending upon their weekly wage for the support of themselves and their families. I only hope that in the case of the Hamilton company it is but a temporary closing down. The Dominion Iron and Steel Company last week passed their dividends. The directors said that this was on account of a depression in the iron situation, but in view of the fact that $141,000,000 worth of iron and steel products were taken into this country last year, there must be a great demand for them at the present time. I understand that only two out of the six furnaces in Sydney are in operation. Perhaps my hon. friends will tell me that the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company has had a very successful career; that they have paid satisfactory dividends, and are not entitled to any special consideration. I understand, from what I consider to be very good authority, that the Nova Scotia Steel and Coal Company have made very small returns out of the manufacture of iron and steel, and that they have made the bulk of their profits in the

shipments of coal and iron ore to German and United States furnaces, which ore, I may say, is mined not in Canada, but in the neighbouring colony of Newfoundland. Last year the Canadian Iron Corporation went into liquidation. This corporation lost millions of dollars because they were unable to withstand the keen competition of United States furnaces and foreign steel plants. The failure of the Canadian Iron and Steel Corporation was a greater factor in the financial circles of London than any other individual occurence of the year in discrediting Canada and Canadian investments.
Was the failure of the Canada Iron Corporation due to the lack of sufficient protection, or to the financial operations of the directors of the company?
I believe that if the industry had had sufficient protection it would not have got into financial trouble.
Would that apply also to the furnaces at Midland and Londonderry?

The Londonderry furnace, I understand, is a subsidiary of the Canada Iron Corporation. The money invested in the Canada Iron Corporation was practically all raised in England, and the loss of these millions of dollars to the British investor is such a serious blow to the present and future development of the Canadian iron and steel industry generally that if we desire to revitalize and rehabilitate this industry, to stimulate and foster its development in the interests of all sections of our community, we must enact some legislative measures, provide some form of adequate protection, or else our Canadian industry wi-11 remain in its present languishing condition, while we are keeping busy foreign iron mines, foreign furnaces, foreign steel plants to supply the ever-increasing requirements of Canada.
I have often thought of the two streams that bind together Canada and the old country; the stream of products from Canada to Great Britain and the stream of capital from Great Britain to Canada. Let this latter stream cease to flow and our Canadian industrial life will inevitably wither and shrink, and in my opinion we cannot continue to secure British capital for this great industry unless we change our attitude towards the present iron and steel situation in Canada.

When in London last fall nay attention was repeatedly called toy British financiers to the very unsatisfactory condition revealed by our trade returns; our imports are so much greater than our exports. The balance of trade is very unfavourable to Canada. The latest return compiled by the Government shows that the total value of our imports for the fiscal year 1912-13 (including bullion and specie) was $686,00.0,000; the total value of our exports, $377,000,000; or, in other words, the balance of trade against Canada amounted to over $300,000,000. To settle this difference we must either draw on our own resources or borrow the money from the old country, because the difference in the balance of trade must be paid in cash. The question of the balance of trade has not hitherto received 'in Canada the general attention paid to it in the older countries, .and consequently, perhaps, it 'is not so generally understood; but it must be realized and admitted that it cannot toe to the advantage of a country to import large quantities of any class of .articles which could and should be manufactured within its own borders from its own natural resources by its own workmen. In his remarks at the last annual meeting of the shareholders ol the Canadian Bank of Commerce, Sir Edmund Walker called attention to these facts and said:
We again draw attention to the large proportion of our imports which consists of iron and steel in various forms, not only as raw materials, hut as manufactured goods. The total value is about $140,000,000. May we once more point out that in the main these articles are used in building or in equipping the country for its future and that such purchases differ in effect from the import of foodstuffs and other rapidly perishing objects. At the same time we regret that the greater part of these iron and steel goods is not made in Canada. To the extent to which by making these goods in Canada we could have lessened the debt represented by the securities we have sold to pay for the difference between imports and exports, we have burdened ourselves for a long time to come.
The question will naturally present itself to you, Mr. Speaker, as to whether we have in Canada the raw material necessary for iron and steel development. Have we iron ores, limestone and coal? Sir, we have them all in abundance. We have iron deposits in the Maritime provinces, in Quebec, in Ontario and in British Columbia. We have large bodies of limestone for fluxing purposes in the Maritime provinces and in the lake Erie and Georgian Bay districts. We have large coal deposits in both

eastern and western Canada and coal can be delivered along the ports of the great lakes at a maximum freight rate of thirty cents per ton.
In the district which I have the honour to represent we have, by actual diamond drill test and development work, proved up millions of tons of iron ore in the Atikokan and Mattawin ranges. In the Atikokan range we have nineteen million tons of ore and twenty-eight million tons in the Mattawin range. In the Michipicoten district of Algoma twenty million tons of iron ore have 'been proved up by actual diamond drill test and development work. In the Woman River district nineteen million tons have been proved up and in the Sudbury district the Moose Mountain properties contain one hundred and ten million tons. This Canadian iron belt, part of which geologists state is an extension of the greatest iron belt in the world, that of the Missabi and Vermilion ranges, alone contains 200 million tons of iron ore, already proved up and capable of being turned into seventy-five million tons of pig iron, a quantity sufficient for all Canadian requirements for fifty years. And, Sir, when we recognize the fact that mining is conducted at from 1,500 to 2,000 feet below the surface in the Vermilion range to the south of the Canadian boundary, it is evident that we may confidently anticipate vast additions to our known iron ore resources when greater development work is undertaken.
Now, Mr. Speaker, does it not strike you that it would be admirable legislation for this Government to do something to foster the development of these great natural resources, so that instead of importing, as we did last year, one hundred - and forty-one million dollars worth of iron and steel products, we would be able to produce a large proportion of this amount in our own country, in our own factories and from our own mines, and thus give employment to thousands of our Canadian workingmen instead of keeping busy foreign mines, foreign factories and foreign steel plants to the advantage of foreign workingmen.
Fully two-thirds of this great iron ore belt of Canada is low-grade magnetite, running from 32% to 36% metallic iron. By magnetic treatment the silicious and earthy impurities can be removed and the metallic contents raised to over 65%, which makes a high grade ore quite suitable for furnace use. This method of treatment has been successfully carried on for years in Norway, Sweden, and New York state. The Moose Mountain Company near Sudbury

has also erected a large concentrating plant for treating these low-grade ores. Next in importance are the large deposits of high sulphur ores which require entirely different treatment to the low-grade magnetite but which when treated are as valuable as the best ores used in the blast furnace. Instead of magnetic separation, specially constructed furnaces are used in which the ore is roasted at a very high temperature which burns or drives off the sulphur contained in the ore. In both cases of ore treatment expensive plants are required and operating costs are necessarily high before the ore is treated and ready for furnace use; the cost ranging from 65 cents to $1.50 per ton, according to ore treated. This additional expense must of necessity be added before this ore can be considered the equal in quality of the imported ores. Consequently our Canadian ores are at a disadvantage compared with the foreign ores, to the extent of 65 cents to $1.50 per ton. The foreign ores are shipped direct from the mines to the furnaces and require no special treatment. When our Canadian ores are subjected to special treatment through the Wedge roasting furnace or other modern process, they are raised to the same high standard as the foreign ores and can be used in the manufacture of all iron and steel products that are imported into Canada.
Now, Mr. Speaker, this vast district which joins together the East and the West is to-day the unproductive part of Canada, but with the development of its iron resources and the investment of millions of dollars in iron and steel plants, and with the employment of thousands of men in the pursuits connected with these industries, this whole section would flourish and become an industrial and productive bond, linking together the East and the West to the advantage and added prosperity of both.
During the past year and a half, Sir, I have visited the Old Country several times, seeking capital for an iron and steel industry. We have in the district of Thunder Bay and Rainy River vast and valuable iron ore deposits and the practicability of using them has been conclusively demonstrated. The city of Port Arthur is anxious for a steel industry, as its credit is tied up with the existing iron furnace in Port Arthur to the extent of $200,000, and it is, I believe, willing to give further assistance to help establish this industry within its borders. In our negotiations with English capitalists, three of the leading iron and steel experts of London have visited, inspected and reported upon the iron ore deposits of the Rainy River and Mattawin districts, and thousands of dollars have been paid out for expert reports and advice, and I can assure this House that if adequate assistance is given to the iron mining and iron and .steel industries, I am now in a position to secure, and will undertake to give the Prime Minister evidence that I can secure at once, ten million dollars for a steel industry in Port Arthur, which will make use of our local Canadian ores for the manufacture of its products. The district in which I live, Mr. Speaker, is but one among the many in Canada that contain great iron ore beds, for the known deposits extend through the Maritime provinces, Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia, and who can say what further deposits remain yet to be discovered in the many remoter regions of this vast country? I believe that if sufficient encouragement is given to our iron and steel development, the results in the Rainy River district will be but indicative of what will happen practically over the whole of Canada. Iron ore mining will be stimulated; idle Canadian furnaces will be put into operation; the erection of new furnaces and steel plants will be undertaken; and this whole industry will thrive and flourish, reaching eventually that degree of importance in the commercial and industrial life of Canada to which it is most undoubtedly entitled, an importance which in the foremost countries of the civilized world, accords it to-day rank second only to agriculture.
Let us now turn for a moment and look at the iron development in the three countries which are in the lead with respect t

1 this particular industry. In the year 1847 Great Britain led the world in the iron and steel industry. Her industries had been built up and placed on a sound footing through protection. At that time the British economists were satisfied that Great Britain would still continue to lead the world. Then Great Britain adopted free trade, and with what result? Both Germany and the United States under high protective policies have fairly outstripped her in the race for supremacy.
Fifty years ago the United States imported practically all her iron and steel. Her infant iron and steel industries were at that time in a languishing condition. She then adopted a high protective tariff with the. result that to-day the United States leads the world in the production of iron and steel. In 1902 the United States produced thirty-five million tons of iron ore and in

1913 sixty million tons. The iron and steel industry of the United States to-day is the largest individual industry of that great republic to the south of us. More money in capital is invested in her iron and steel industry than in any other of her industries. The total amount of iron and steel produced in the United States last year was valued at $1,755,000,000 and this industry gave employment to 375,000 persons and paid out over $265,000,000 in wages. If we take into consideration all the more highly elaborated articles that are produced from iron and steel, the total capital investment in the iron and steel industry in the United States, taken from the latest census report of 1909, is $3,573,000,000; the total value of the products produced is $3,163,000,000 ,and the average number of wage earners is 1,025,000.
In 1890 Great Britain produced eight million tons of pig iron and Germany 4,600,000 tons. In 1912 Great Britain produced 8,900,000 tons and Germany 17,800,000. Germany at the present time is the second greatest producer of iron and steel in the world, and through the protection which she has afforded her industries and the special freight rates granted by the Government on the national railways to iron and steel products, she has developed iron deposits which do not average any higher in metallic contents than our Canadian ores. Mr. Dawson in his history of the iron and steel development of Germany states that ' their iron ores do not average over thirty-five per cent metallic iron.'
Now let us look at the iron ore situation in Canada. In 1902 Canada produced 400,000 tons of iron ore and in 1912, 216,000 tons, or a reduction of forty-six per cent. In 1902 Canada imported 560,000 tons of iron ore and in 1912 she imported over two million tons of iron ore, an increase of over two hundred and fifty per cent.
Next let us bake the manufacture of pig iron in Canada. In 1912 Canada manufactured one million tons of pig iron practically all from foreign OTes and she imported 272,000 tons of pig iron; or a total of 1,272,000 tons of pig iron was used in Canada last year. To produce this amount of pig iron would require 2,500,000 tons of iron ore, 750,000 tons of limestone and 2,100,000 tons of coal; which makes a total tonnage of 5,350,000 tons. This alone to the navigation and transportation companies equals the freight in tonnage on nearly two hundred million bushels of wheat. It is nearly as great a tonnage as was shipped in grains of all sorts through the lake 
ports of Port Arthur and Fort William during the navigation season of 1913, which amounted to 205,000,000 bushels.
At this point, Sir, it occurs to me that you may perhaps wonder how, seeing that the manufacture of pig iron and certain steely products has increased in Canada, I can justify my declaration that the industry is in a languishing and deplorable condition. I am aware that the manufacture of pig iron in Canada has increased; that the output of steel rails, steel rods and other steel commodities has increased; that one or two establishments in close proximity to ample markets of high-grade foreign ore have been able to increase their production and by the use of that ore to keep their heads above water. But, Sir, I would ask you to recall the 250 per cent increase in importations of foreign ores, the fact that in ten years our imports of iron and steel products have amounted from $33,000,000 to over $140,000,000, the still greater sum of $300,000,000 against Canada in the balance of trade when over a quarter of our importations consists of iron and steel products, the many furnaces now standing idle, the vast ore beds unmined and unexploited; and I think you must admit that my statement is justified and in no sense an exaggeration.
What has been the attitude of the Governments of Canada towards the iron industry? Both Liberal and Conservative Governments have been favourable to a policy of fostering and developing this industry. Regardless of differences in policies on other questions, regardless of cleavage within parties, there has been an earnest endeavour by both parties to stimulate -this great industry. At times, it is true, that there was a difference of opinion as to how the best results could be "obtained, but from the history of past legislation it must be admitted that this industry received support from both great political parties in Canada. But, Sir, neither party went far enough and neither party gave to the industry the protection necessary to enable it to entrench itself securely, to withstand the competition from more strongly established foreign industries, whose governments secured for them by hign tariffs their own home markets and who were thus able to make use of Canada as a dumping ground for their surplus.
In the year 1883 the Conservative Government passed legislation authorizing the payment of a bounty of $1.50 per ton on all pig iron manufactured from Canadian ores.

la 1894, Mr. Foster, our present Minister of Trade and Commerce, introduced a Bill increasing the bounty to $2 per ton. In 1897, after the Liberals came into poweT, they reduced the customs protection, in some cases as much as 75 per cent and in others from 25 per cent to 50 per cent, and in 1897 Mr. Fielding introduced a Bill increasing the bounties to $3 per ton on all pig iron manufactured from Canadian ores and autnorizing a bounty of $2 per ton on all pig iron made in Canada from foreign ores; or, if pig iron were produced from a mixture of Canadian and foreign ores, then the product would be entitled to the bounty of $3 and $2 respectively on the proportions of Canadian and foreign ores used. In introducing the Bill to increase the bounties on pig iron Mr. Fielding said:
The object is, to some extent at all events, to make amends to the iron interests for, the loss they will undoubtedly sustain by the lowering- of the duties. I have no doubt there are in the minds of some of the hon. gentlemen objections to the system of bounties, but we have thought that as these interests were established and large capital invested in them, it was only reasonable that we should give them a chance to see what development might be possible for a few years longer. We have, therefore, come to the conclusion, in lieu of the higher duties which were formerly received, to ask the House to grant them increased bounties-
Mr. Fielding and the Liberal party when in opposition were not in favour of bounties, but when they came into power they recognized the importance of the iron industry to the development of the country and were anxious to stimulate and encourage it. They increased the bounties, therefore, to a higher figure than had ever before been paid in Canada and Mr. Fielding said that the object was
-to some extent at all events to make amends to the iron interests for the loss they will undoubtedly sustain by the lowering of the duties.
Mr. Fielding was perfectly correct. The iron industry did undoubtedly sustain a great loss through the lowering of the customs duties; a loss which shattered the hopes and blasted the fortunes of many Canadians. But the late Government was earnestly desirous of helping the iron development and in 1897, 1899, 1904 and 1907 brought down legislation mitigating, at least to some extent, by means of bounties the loss to which the iron and steel industry was subjected by the lowering of the customs duties. Again I repeat the words of Mr. Fielding:
We have, therefore, come to the conclusion, in lieu of the higher duties which were in force, to ask the House to grant them increased bounties.	_
Sir, the greatly lower duties to which Mr. Fielding referred are still in force, but the bounties are no longer being paid.
In 1907, in introducing further bounties on finished products, Mr. Fielding said:
X think it will be generally admitted that if there is any industry in the country which deserves encouragement-if we are to adopt the principle of aiding any industry by protection in the form of bounties or of customs duties or in any other form-it will hardly be questioned that the iron and steel industry should receive the favourable consideration of the House. A country which possesses large resources and fails to develop them, would certainly not be a progressive country.
Mr. Fielding also said:
There is, I think, an erroneous impression that the iron and steel industries are protected to a particularly large degree. I think that is a mistake. X have no doubt that some of our farming friends will be surprised if I tell them that the protection afforded to the iron and steel indutry is not so great as the protection afforded to some line of agricultural products, but such is the case.
The Finance Minister of the late Administration then gave figures showing the low rates of customs duties on iron and steel products, and said:
These are very low rates of duty. They would not be considered a protection in any other line of industry and if there were not any bounty to supplement them, they certainly would not be any substantial protection to the steel industry.
Mr. Fielding then closed this part of his argument by stating that he believed that every dollar paid out in bounties came back to the treasury of the country. He said:
In view of the results which have been accomplished by the continuance of this policy for many years, first under one Government and then under another, even if it had cost the country a very considerable sum of money, I think a good case can be made out to justify the outlay having regard to the importance which the iron and steel industry will always bear to the development of the business of the country. But, I think it is as capable of proof as most things are capable of proof in an argument of this character, that every dollar which has been paid out of the treasury for some years past in connection with the development of the iron and steel industry has come back to the treasury from the general development of the country in connection with the establishment of these great industries.
From legislation which was introduced by the Conservatives up to 1896 and from legislation introduced by the Liberals subsequent to 1896., it has been clearly

A resolution was passed last week by The Canadian Mining Institute, a nonpolitical organization which deals with all the mines and ores in this country. The resolution sets out that:
The Canadian Mining Institute, in annual meeting assembled, beg to direct the attention of the federal Government to the fact that the iron ore industry of Canada is handicapped by reason that there have not yet been found, in this country, extensive deposits of the same high grade ore as are easily mined in the neighbouring republic, in Newfoundland and Cuba and which necessitates the importation of 94 per cent of all iron ore smelted in Canada; whereas, it is the conviction of the Canadian Mining Institute that such deposits ought, by increased endeavour to be found, therefore we most respectfully request that the Dominion Government will, through its proper channels, provide the necessary means for the accomplishment of this most desired end, the realization of which will add more than anything else to the economic wealth of the Dominion.
The Canadian Mining Institute say that the development of our iron ore deposits will add more than anything else to the economic wealth of the Dominion of Canada.
I desire also to read a resolution placed on the Order Paper of the provincial legislature by Mr. Gamey, as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the iron industry is one of prime importance and its satisfactory development within our borders a matter of national concern; mat, notwithstanding the fact that there are immense deposits of iron ore in Ontario and the other provinces of the Dominion now lying Idle or but little worked, the great and growing market for manufacturers of iron and steel, and also the demand for iron ore for smelting purposes, are largely met by importations from abroad and especially from the United States; therefore, be it resolved that, in the opinion of this House, the development of Canada would be stimulated and public interest promoted by the granting of such a measure of assistance by the Parliament of Canada as would place the iron and steel industry of this country on an assured and permanent footing.
In conclusion, I would point out that the granting of special aid by the Government to important industries is and has long been a settled policy in this country. I could turn to our steamship and transportation lines, to our fisheries, to our lead mines and even to our agriculture, and show you how this industry has been fostered by subsidies and land grants and the development of our natural resources encouraged by bounties, high duties, hatcheries, experimental farms and various other means. But I would not weary the House with figures, for surely an industry which is the foundation of every other industry-which is the basic fibre of our in-

dustrial activity; which in the foremost countries of the civilized world vies in importance even with agriculture-surely the encouragement of such an industry is worthy of being judged on its own merits. We consider ourselves a progressive country. The pulses of our nationality beat fast with youth and ambition. We claim that the twentieth century belongs to Canada. Yet, in spite of the example of what has been accomplished in other countries, in the face of our vast iron resources lying idle and neglected, in the face of our idle blast furnaces, in the face of the 141 millions of imports of iron and steel products which could be and should be manufactured in this country by our own workmen from our own resources, what are we doing to take advantage of our opportunities? What are we doing to prove our progressiveness? What are we doing to promote the welfare of this supremely important industry? I repeat the words of the Hon. Mr. Fielding:	' A
country which possesses large resources and fails to develop them, would certainly not be a progressive country,' and with confidence I leave the answer to my questions to the judgment of this House.

I could not help reflecting, as I listened to the questions which my hon. friend put to the House just before he resumed his seat, that the answer to them would have been very different if the result of the last election had been different. He said: What are we doing to develop the industries of the country? Well, I must say that under this Government we are not doing very much. But if the result of the last election had been different, the answer to these questions would have been different. We would have been opening the markets of the world to our produce; we would have been setting free industries, and we would have been making a prosperous Canada. That is what we would have been doing.
My hon. friend has told a tale, in the most able manner from his own point of view, and in a very pleasant manner, which must be harrowing to the soul of every patriotic Canadian. I could not help regretting that he did not tell this tale before the Speech from the Throne was composed, because I almost think that if that tale had been told before the Government had composed the Speech from the Throne, they would not have talked about a slight depression in Canada. I wish that the Prime Minister and my hon. friend the

Minister of Finance had consulted my hon. friend from Thunder Bay and Rainy River (Mr. Carrick) before they made their speeches on the Address. I can not help thinking that, if they had had the information which my hon. friend has just given to the House, they would have been very much less severe in their speeches upon my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition when he attempted to place a truthful picture of the conditions of this country before the Parliament and the people. ' Deplorable and depressed condition of the industries of Canada ' is what we hear from my hon. friend from Rainy River and Thunder Bay. Well, it took the advocates of the National Policy eighteen years to produce that state of affairs before, but we have got a much more clever Government in power; they have done it, their own friends being witnesses, in two years. I deplore this, but I wonder if my hon. friend doe3 not think that there is a perfectly natural explanation in his own remarks of how this condition has been brought about. He voted, and he induced h:s constituents to vote, for the depression of *iie industry of this country which he himself admits is our primary and greatest industry; for he only claimed the iron industry to be secondary to the great interest o! agriculture. Why did he seek the support of the people to depress that industry? Does it not occur to him that if he took the deliberate step of shutting up the markets of the world, or keeping shut up the markets of the world, against the agricultural products of this country and so depressing Canada's primary industry, the secondary industry as a natural result was bound to be depressed also? Why, the very thing he uses in his classification and description of industries gives him the clear explanation of all the phenomena which are so depressing to him as they are to all of us.
In this connection I could not understand my hon. friend being so much put out by the importation of a huge amount of iron in various forms from foreign countries, especially the United States. For I recollect an argument used two and a quarter years ago, and elaborated at great length in this House by possibly the most brilliant ornament of this House, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster), whom I am glad to see back from his wanderings, and that argument was that reciprocity would be a bad thing because it would exhaust the natural resources of Canada. I submit to my hon. friend that
if we were saving up our own resources, his object was to exhaust the resources of other countries. And when this exhaustion is going on, is it not a matter of rejoicing- and especially when you are exhausting the resources of the country for which you have no particular affection, and .with which, by the way, we wanted ' no truck or trade.' Well, that by the way.
Now, I should like to elaborate just a little the arguments on bounties and upon this whole matter. My hon. friend's speech is an apt demonstration of the fact that there can be no greater anachronism than to apply the term ' national ' to the policy of protection. It is not a ' national ' policy, it never was; it has always been sectional, and selfish at that. It must have been observed by every one present that while my hon. friend set out with a number of figures and references about the iron trade, he gravitated, slowly perhaps, but absolutely surely, to Thunder Bay and Fort William, and he ended there. That is to say, he was sectional in his very thinking. He was not thinking of Canada in the long run; he did premise his speech with that to make it respectable-and very respectable he made it-but he got to Thunder Bay and Rainy River and Fort William, and that is the place he was talking to in this debate. Protection is always sectonal. There are people in Nova Scotia who support this policy, but to do it they have to forget Canada and think only of Nova Scotia. And so with portions of Ontario. What a misnomer to apply the term 'national' to such a policy. It is sectional as to locality, and I think it is sectional in another sense, because I think it is meant to benefit a particular section of the community. The suggestion of my hon. friend is made to benefit a very particular section of the community and I am not sure that that section will receive a great deal of sympathy from the great mass of the people of Canada at this time, and it certainly is not likely to receive a great deal of sympathy from the farmers who are the exponents and practisers of the primary industry of the country and who were prevented from making greater gains in their business by a trade 'pact which would not have harmed any man, woman or child in Canada, but would have helped the great industry which now comes before us for help. I am not sure there are not some sectional investors behind this project. I am told that the stock of iron and steel companies is not quite as good a thing as it was. I do not follow these things very

much myself; I am in the happy position of not being troubled with surplus wealth- and 1 use the word 'troubled' advisedly, for it is nothing but a nuisance; it causes people to think wrongly in their economics and to act wrongly in life, and the love of it, we are told, is the root of all evil. But I read the papers and get some information, and I understand that there is a great decline in the value of the stocks of these companies.	I am sure
the inhabitants of Canada who are absolutely most anxious for something to be done along the line suggested by my hon. friend are precisely these investors. I do not want to hurt any investors, but I am not anxious to help them at the expense of other people and at the expense of the industries which have made and are making Canada, The fact of the matter is that if an industry is in that particular position, and if it be true-and I have no reason to doubt w-hat my hon. friend says-that it requires from seventy-five cents to $1.50 per ton more to handle iron ore in this country than in the United States, then I gather from the facts that these men made investment in a business which was very bad to invest in in this country at this juncture of its development-and when Canada gave bounties to that business it embarked upon a losing concern-and that these people deserve no particular consideration from this country. The whole system of bounties, the whole system of protection, receives its severest condemnation in the facts my hon. friend gave me in this connection. He asks us in effect to take money from industries which are paying because they are suitable to the country and which pay under freedom and without the help of protection-he asks the Government of this country to go to these paying industries which would most surely build up the prosperity of the country and abstract money from them to hand it over to an industry which, the very facts he gives us show, is not suited to the stage of development at which Canada has arrived. It cannot be demonstrated according to sound economics that it is profitable for Canada to go into that industry. FaT better-follow the argument of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and keep these particular resources and make the exchanges we are making and can make of an immense surplus of agricultural produce for every kind of surplus that is produced more profitably and easily in other countries of the world. The result will be that both countries will be richer by the transaction.
[Mr. M. Clark. 3
I wonder if my hon. friend, when he quoted the language of Sir Charles Tupper about the support of the iron trade being necessary to attract capital to this country, ever thought in what form that capital reaches us. From his saying that the balance of trade against us needs to be settled in cash, I really inferred he thought that he got money sometimes from another country and that this surplus capital that we bring into Canada comes in the shape of money. If he did think that, or does think it, or if any other member of this House thinks it, let me at once disabuse his mind of that thought.
Every particle of the borrowed money that we bring into this country comes in in the shape of those very goods which my hon. friend wants to debar. The other day Mr. Asquith took the chair at a lecture delivered by one of the first economists of Britain upon this very question, and on that occasion both the chairman and the speaker were emphatic in the declaration that every particle of borrowed capital that came to this country came in the shape of goods. So that the Government, in a protectionist country such as Canada, is really the greatest foe of its own theory and its own policy of protection. All the surplus money that we have been bringing into Canada, except what comes in as settlers' effects, comes in in the shape of goods. My hon. friend seems, therefore, to land himself into a contradiction on that point. He says we have got to build up the iron industry at home in order to attract the necessary capital from abroad, but a great deal of that necessary capital is coming in in the shape of the very iron and steel products connected with the industry which he wants to build up at home. That is a sample of the economic contradictions that abound whenever you take up the subject of protection, because the whole thing is an economic fallacy from beginning to end; it is wrong, and no amount of practice of it will ever put it right.

In the hurried remarks that I made before dinner, I referred to the balance of trade which had been spoken of by my hon. friend from Rainy River. It has been pointed out to me that the statement I made might easily be misunderstood. I said, very hurriedly, that when we borrow money from England we import the whole of what we borrow in the shape of goods. I might have been misunderstood as indicating that we get these goods from Great Britain. Of course, that would be an impossibility because the balance of trade does not run that way as between Great Britain and ourselves. Everyone who has an elementary knowledge of these matters knows that the exchange is not always an exchange directly between the two countries concerned. It might take place through a great many countries. We borrow money from England, and that money comes to us in the shape of a draft. The draft represents capital which is in Great Britain and which, so far as cash value is concerned, remains in Great Britain. The draft, wherever it goes first, arrives ultimately in Great Britain and becomes an order upon the British market for goods. That is the point. The draft may first go to the United States and buy goods from the United States, but in that case the United States does not give away goods to Canada for a piece of paper. It passes the draft on, and the draft gets back ultimately to the country from Which it came, where the exchange value resides and where the goods are bought.
I want to say a few more words on this	question of bounties.	The
fundamental objections to bounties are two in number.	The first is that
they are of necessity unjust to producers in lines other than that to which the bounty is paid, and equally unjust to the consumers of the country. On the face of it what can justify taking money from the masses of the people to encourage production along a certain line when that money would go farther in the purchase of the required goods in some other country? What actually happens is not that the money would go further, but that some other products of Canada would go 96
farther, because in the commercial exchanges between countries, if we import iron and steel, jve inevitably export something else which we can produce more easily than we can iron and steel, to purchase the iron and steel. That is the inevitable process of trade. The money comes from somewhere to pay this bounty; it does not drop from the heavens; and where alone can it come from, where does it come from? It comes from the consumers of the country who are themselves producers in other lines. No one can shift that position; it is a position of the most absolute injustice as between one industry and the other industries of the country.
That is how the cost of living is raised. We appoint commissions to inquire into the cause of the high cost of living. There is no doubt whatever about what is the cause of the high cost of living, as I said in a previous debate in this session. If at this time we wanted to meet the real trouble that is afflicting the Canadian people, we should introduce bounties on beef and not on iron and steel. We have no beef in this country; our beef has all been drawn off from us. I submit to the hon. member for Rainy River that there was a great deal of beef used in'this country before any iron and steel, and, like agriculture, it is a more primary necessity of the human being. Now, I put it to my hon. friend, representing an industrial community while I represent an agricultural-if he will be a Canadian for a moment and not an inhabitant of one particular district in Canada- if he proposes seriously to this House that we should take money from the whole of the Canadian people to hand over-and we have already done it to the tune of seventeen or eighteen millions-to the industry in which his constituency is interested, by what process of logic or of justice does he refuse to me the same consideration for the industry of Alberta, which is largely a beef industry? If we look to the needs of the people, there is more need to encourage the production of beef than the production of iron and steel, and I would ask my hon. friend on what ground he would refuse the one and not the other. It is impossible to meet that argument in any other way than to say, as my friend must at this moment feel inclined to say: I will give you a bounty on beef too. If he would make that admission I would say that we had better not begin the process at all. I will produce the beef 'and he can produce the iron



and steel, and we will both be self-respecting and self-reliant Canadians.
Viewing this thing from the national rather than from the local aspect, there is a grave reason in tihe present condition of Canada why we should support agriculture as the primary industry of this country. Nothing is more serious at the present time than the depopulation of our rural districts. I made a trip recently in the province of Nova Scotia and I found a splendid set of people, but I found that their population was almost stationary. We are told that the rural population of Ontario is declining. Many here know of a time-I have read and heard of it-when the people were leaving eastern Canada by the hundred thousand for the United States. To-day we can carry this process farther west. I was shocked to receive a paper the other day from a point in Southern Alberta, which said that it stated with reluctance, although it had to state it as the truth, that in the district of Grassy Lake there were 20 per cent fewer people than there were two years ago.
Of farmers?

Yes, it is a farming
district. The process is going on under my own eyes. I cam count the number of men who have left the district in which 1 have lived ever since I came to Canada. In some cases they have gone to our cities, in other cases to the United States. I submit that is a very serious condition. Careful observers of human affairs in other lands are looking at what is going on in Canada and trying to learn lessons from it.
I want to read an extract from an article by Samuel Evans, chairman of the Grown Mines, Limited, South Africa, on protection in British South Africa. I think all who are Imperialists will want to hear what this prominent citizen of South Africa has to say upon the .subject:
The tendency of population to gravitate to cities is no doubt characteristic of modern civilization, but the experience of Australia and Canada-
And I submit that when calm thinkers of British South Africa are studying our economic conditions we surely ought to be studying them here.
-the experience of Australia and Canada appears to show that this movement is accelerated by protection, as protection bolsters up industries which are carried on in towns, and it handicaps the farmers by taxing their requirements in order to foster such industries.

That is the comment of a highly cultured South African upon conditions which he has learnt there are prevailing in Canada, and I submit that that is something which should make us who are responsible for the Government of Canada, each in his own degree, think very seriously indeed before we listen to a suggestion such as my hon. friend has thrown out; because his suggestion is specifically to do this very thing which is condemned by Mr. Evans: It is to bolster up an industry in a town at the expense of the rural population and the agricultural interests of the country.
The second objection to bounties is that they are doubtfully helpful to the industries that receive them. That would, I think, follow from theoretical reasoning upon the point. I have given these reasons to the House before. If I wanted to spoil a boy of mine I would not need to lay traps to lead him into immorality; I would only need to give him plenty of money to spend and the boy would be spoilt. The same law applies to human beings of a more advanced age, and applies to the industries of the country. I referred just now to the fact that I was in Nova Scotia recently. I think I told the House in the only previous remarks I have addressed to it this session, that I found that all this money that is being paid into the steel industry of Nova Scotia is by no means as successful as it should be. Two shops were closed at Sydney when I was there, and I applied to the courteous manager who showed me over the works, as to the cause. He said it was because they had no orders; but I learned of another very interesting thing: that since the orders fell off for the production of the heavier plant of that steel works, the capable people managing the works had immediately turned their attention to the production of nails. I was very much interested to see that they turned out splendid specimens of all classes of nails, from the finest to the very largest spikes. I ask the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance to this-he knows it all in theory, or at least he knew it a long time ago when he used to read Adam Smith, but I am afraid he has not read that author in recent times as much as he should have done-I wish to call his attention to this concrete example of what the absence of bounties has done for this industry. Here is a case where the federal bounty, or at any rate, the failure of the lines in which they had been operating as a result of the bounty, led to these people falling back on their own ability and in-

genuity, which after all are the qualities on which men should rely in life, and introducing a perfectly different line of production and doing it as well as it is done anywhere in the civilized world. That proves positively what the effect of these bounties is upon industries. I should like to ask my hon. friend from Rainy River (Mr. Car-rick) or any one who follows in this discussion to. tell me how any amount of bounty will produce orders. My hon. friend is beginning the development of his country at the wrong end. I can quite understand how the payment of bounties by the million will raise tne price of stock, especially for speculative purposes. If it was known here to-night that the bounties were going to be given, I should expect to see a rise of the stocks-a watery rise-noted in to-morow morning's paper. I can understand that, and I can understand how you can pay dividends out of bounties, if the bounties are big enough. This is not the first country in which these economic follies have been indulged in. In the country from which I come, years before I was born, they used to pay dividends to fishermen for catching fish, and it became a familiar saying that the fishermen went to sea not to catch the fish but to catch the bounties. But I cannot see how bounties would enable this steel works to get orders. I may be blind, but I would be glad if somebody would tell me how bounties are going to bring orders.
The fact is, in my humble, opinion 'that free access to the United States market two and a half years ago would have gone far to obviate the necessity of my hon. friend making the speech he did this afternoon, whether we have regard to the condition of the country which he described as existing or to the remedy which he proposes for that condition. If we had got that market two years sooner than we did, there is one thing certain, and that is that we would have got a better price tor our stock two years sooner than we did.
I do not know what the Government a-e going to do about the matter of markets below the Tine, but if they want to develop this country they must develop foreign markets. That is the way to build up your steel industry. We who are occupying those vast areas which constitute a heritage such as no country in the world ever came into are not out there for sport. The people who are raising cattle are not out there, as I have told some audiences in this country, to conduct zoological gardens. The only reason they produce cattle is that they are 96}
able to sell them, and if you close the market against their product you shut down the lands, you lead to the result which I have pointed out as existing down in Southern Alberta, and if you close down the primary industries the secondary industries can never graw up. These are two main objections to bounties: they are unjust, and they are not helpful but a hindrance to the industries to which they are given. It is inevitable, according to human nature, that such should be the case.
I cannot help adding that the proposition of my hon. friend is particularly inopportune at this period of Canada's history and in the condition which we all unfortunately know to be prevailing at the present time. I am the last man in the world to want to exaggerate that condition. One of the most pestilential by-products of the tariff reform agitation in Great Britain was that people came from Great Britain with false ideas about the empire and said things condemnatory of our land which were extremely bad hearing for Britishers living abroad Therefore I should be the last in the world to wish to follow an example of that kind. I do not think it is the part of a good patriot to decry his own country or to paint in too dark colours the condition of that country, and certainly he is not a patriot who does it for political purposes. My hon. friend opposite, however, has made it inevitable that I should put it up to him that this ia a most inopportune time for the very reasons which are to be found in his statement as to the condition of the country. I think that if he had reflected a moment he would have thought of the old proverb that it is no use begging from those who a"e ready to steal. I have already pointed out to him that this money must come from somewhere, and I do not know an industry that could not do with a bounty at the present time.
Thanks to the President of the United States and his tariff, we have a little help in the matter of cattle in Alberta, and vfre are able to stand on our own feet in that province; but it is a questionable thing if wheat can be produced at the prices which are being paid for it. Surely, if that be the case, my hon. friend must see that an application for bounties on wheat would be a much more sensible thing to think about than an application for bounties upon iron ore. People cannot eat iron ore. The production of iron is a secondary consideration altogether. We need iron, and steel, butT it is not necessary that we should make them. It is absolutely necessary that we should raise food, and if bounties are
Do not take that back.
M,r. ARTHURS: Has my (hon. friend the. figures of what the workingmen in England receive 'in similar industries?

I am so used to my hon. friend's interruptions that I would be glad to go into the question with him. I do not mind a diversion if we are both in order. I am a little disappointed, however, when any one on the other side wants to make capital by running down the mother country. It is a revelation of a new side to my hon. friend's .character.
Answer the question.

I will get to the question. With regard to the remuneration of labour, if that is what my hon. friend wants me to go -into, I shall be very glad to -take a little excursion with him. I would begin my excursion by -saying -this, that there are in the British House of Commons forty labour members who -are the aristocrats of the world of labour. At the head of them is my old personal friend, Mr. Burt, who, if he is spared until next month, will have sat in th-e House fox forty years, who was -described by Lord Grey, our -late Governor General, as the finest gentleman he ever met, who was raised to the Treasury Bench by Mr. Gladstone, -and who is the father of the House of Commons. He and -the others who constitute the forty labour men hav-e had it for their duty, on behalf of those who first sent them to Parliament, to study labour -conditions the world over.
They have not missed a point in the case; they have studied it with the best brains they could bring to bear upon it; and every one of them is as bad a freetrader as I am, because he knows -that protection does not raise the wages of labour. If my hon. friend is not content with that little excursion, I can give him numbers of other facts upon which he can build more correct information and opinions with regard to -the remuneration of workmen under protection.
We would like to have the figures.

I will give my hon. friend the figures. Forty labour members-there is a figure; does he -set his judgment against the whole forty? But I will give him some figures from nearer home. The hon. member does not seem to be impressed by the labour members of the British Parliament.
I will call gentlemen of -more august posi-IMr. M. Clark.]
tion from nearer home. I am glad I have been diverted to th-e question of how far protection, whether in the shape of bounty or of tariffs, raises the wages of workmen. This question has been discussed in the United States for the last sixty years, and until lately they believed what the hon. gentleman still believes. My hon. friend is a stand-patter, but the worst thing about a stand-patter is that while he is -standing pat the world moves away from him. In the last presidential election in the United States this question of wages was dealt with by three very important citizens of that great community. In the first place, Mr. Roosevelt had something to say -about it, as he will always have -something to say about affairs -if lie happens to be around at the time. Mt. Roosevelt, who had been a high pri-est in the protectionist temple for a good many years, -said: I want to see more of the rewards of industry finding its w-ay into the pay envelope. I would like to ask the hon. member for Parry Sound what Mr. Roosevelt meant 'by that. If hi-s words meant anything, th-ey meant an admission on his part that enough of the wages did not get -into the pay envelope.
Did he-

Let my hon. friend not
deal with half a case. He will have the chance of speaking all night, if he wishes, after I have finished. Mr. Taft came along, and he dealt with the question in which my hon. friend is interested-and let it not be forgotten that he was holding office at the time as the high priest in the protectionist temple. He said: ' Mr. Roosevelt says that he wants more of the rewards of industry to go into the pay envelope. I want to tell him it cannot be done.' It is bad enough for Mr. Roosev<Bt to state that it is not being done, but Mr. Taft said it could not be done, and added:	' And I
want to tell Mr. Roosevelt that until he shows how it can be done, hi-s programme is for show and not for sale.' These are very high authorities for my hon. friend from Parry Sound. But he wants figures. Well, I propose to give him figures, from the third of the gentlemen to whom I have referred, the successful candidate for the Presidency. Mr. Woodrow Wilson came along in the same election and went down to Lawrence, in Massachusetts, and he said to the people there: ' They have been telling you for generations that protection raises your wages; you get a dollar a day and you are paying thirty cents a pound

for beefsteak-I hope my hon. friend is getting the figures; more figures than steak for these workmen. I am not giving my own language, but am quoting from the present President of the United States about the beautiful results to the workmen of the United States that flow from this so-called national policy. Mr. Wilson went on: 'They say protection raises your wages; I see that it raises the cost of your food, but I do not see that it raises your wages; and you are in a position to tell these who come along with the statement that it does raise your wages, that that is a grand piece of humbug.' I commend that to my hon. friend as a point from which he might begin to study economics so far as they teach the effect of protection upon wages.
